Medical Xenophobia

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Hospitals have become the latest epicentre of xenophobic friction. Is the unconstitutional maltreatment of foreign pregnant women in South African medical facilities fuellin the fire of xenophobia?

Unique Selling Point:
And what of the victims?

All over various media we’ve seen Dr Phophi Ramathuba MEC for Health in Limpopo, lambasting a Zimbabwean patient for taking up bed space and resources in a Limpopo Hospital. She further rants, that the Zimbabwian government should be paying for her. She makes an example of her recent trip to Canada, and goes on to say, that if she were to fall ill there, she would have to pay for it. Her entourage laughs with her as she continues to berate the patient. Before you know it, Operation Dudula are trying to prevent foreigners from entering Kalafong Hospital in Attridgeville, asking for their permits and papers and refusing them entrance if they are foreign. A stand-off and violence erupt as EFF oppose this action. But medical xenophobia has been an ongoing problem in South Africa and over the last couple of years it has been even more evident in labour wards. Here women are mistreated because they are foreigners but are too afraid to speak out. Not only do they fear for their own life but the unborn baby they are bringing into the world.

Section 4(3) of the National Health Act says "All pregnant and breastfeeding women and children under the age of six are eligible for free health care services at public clinics or hospitals."

In this very personal story of pain and humiliation we explore the indignity that befalls women of foreign origin at the hands of South Africa’s public health care system in the wake of xenophobic rhetoric which is escalating conveniently and alarmingly before elections.


Summary:
Gertie, a Zimbabwian woman who wishes to remain anonymous. Has been living and working in South Africa as a domestic for the last 20 years. She fell pregnant with her 3rd child in South Africa three years ago. She went to Thembisa Hospital for obstetric care. Even as she got into the ambulance while in labour, the Venda ambulance driver warned her that they don’t like foreigners at the hospital, and that if she was goaded or badly treated she should keep quiet and not incite the hospital staff, as it would be even more dangerous for her. Gertie wanted to have natural child birth, but it was at this point that the nursing staff started to threaten her, saying if she were to have natural childbirth, they would leave her to die, referring to her as “these Zimbabwian women are very stubborn”. Gertie felt humiliated and afraid, not knowing if she was going to live or die, giving birth to her daughter. She did what the paramedic told her to do, and when she was shouted at, she just kept quiet. She gave birth to a beautiful daughter, but never went back to the hospital for any post natal care. Subsequently because of all the xenophobia, she sent her other children back to Zimbabwe, fearing for their lives.

This is one story of many women who are suffering in South Africa’s obstetric health care. Many are crying out that this is unconstitutional and inhumane. Activists are angry and point to the constitution that all people should have access to healthcare even if they are undocumented or foreign.

Prof Alex Van den Heever condemns these actions, and blames it on a lack of policy that was never put in place in 1994 in conjunction with neigbouring counties.


Further information:
The knock-on effect according to Dr Manyonga, a Zimbabwean obstetrician resident in South Africa for over 20 years, is that women are opting for back-room or home births, which in itself causes complications. Moreover after giving birth these foreign nationals don’t get their children immunised for fear of being victimised. In the long term this could cause serious health hazards for the entire population. Like an outbreak of measles.

We explore the route of this deep seated xenophobia and why pregnant mothers are particularly vulnerable, we challenge the Department of Health on their perspective and why Dr Ramathuba’s comments although they may be vested in truth, go against the Hippocratic Oath and is this a culture in health care that the department is willing to perpetuate?

Dr Manyonga wants to be part of a solution, realising a few years back how inefficient obstetric treatment is in the public sector, not only for foreign women but mainly for South African women, he set up an entire service, which extends to engagements with private clinics and the services of midwives, creating a network of affordable obstetric care. His venture was curtailed during COVID, but now it is back in full swing, and what he has found is that more and more foreign women are seeking this service for fear of what lies in the public sector hospitals.

Dr Manyonga is concerned with Dr Ramathuba’s comments, particularly as he states, that was a conversation that should have been had at a higher level, rather than breaking the patient doctor confidentiality. He also addresses the deeper reasons for this influx of patients from Zimbabwe, as the health care system there is virtually nonexistent.

Doula Bev, knows first hand of incidents of maltreatment. She wants to remain anonymous, but can attest to the many instances of maltreatment of women she has helped ( I may not interview her, if I can get an on camera interview with a midwife that I am trying to get hold of)



I am hoping Flora Banda will give us an interview even though it will probably also be anonymous, concerning a member of her family who they say died shortly after giving birth to twins due to hospital neglect. She was a Malawian national and undocumented.

Yolanda Dumpson, whose story was covered by Health-E, is worried about speaking more because she now fears xenophobic attacks – but it looks like we have other case studies of our own.

Sibongile Tshabalala from Treatment Action Campaign (TAC) who are condemning this inhumane treatment of people. Sibongile can be interviewed as an activist.

As an expert, Professor Alex Van Den Heever, says the problem is that since 1994 there no policy has been defined between the SADC countries and this needs to be addressed by government.

The National Department of Health needs to address the issues of what happened this week. Why was the MEC allowed to speak the way she did? Why is there is so much xenophobia, and what is their position, especially, what is being done to protect pregnant women who constitutionally should be able to expect equal healthcare in South African public hospitals

We can narrow down the interviews in frying session so that there are not too many.

As Carte Blanche highlighted during its medical series, South Africa’s national health system is suffering from dysfunctionality... a baby is about to be born and in many cases hospital staff are more worried about nationality, ids, hospital cards and paperwork than they are about the welfare of mother and baby. It’s not like a woman about to give birth is arriving at a hospital with a cough.

Is it endemic corruption because it siphons off much needed funding? Or are foreigners using up resources meant for South Africans? Many citizens blame foreign patients for the lack of care afforded them. And the tensions are starting to boil. Opponents to this attitude are groups that quote our constitution - Section 27 of South Africa's Constitution states the right to access health care services is one of the basic human rights for everyone. This includes reproductive health care services. Others campaign for tighter border controls to ease the issue of illegal foreigners.

Whatever the argument or motivation, the fallout is being felt most harshly by the vulnerable. And if you were in their position would you have stayed in Zimbabwe for instance or seek care elsewhere? The Zimbabwean health system has crumbled and hard hit are expectant mothers... United Nations data shows that there are 37.9 deaths per 1 000 live births in Zimbabwe. A stark contrast to data for Zimbabwe's neighbours... in Botswana - 28.8 deaths per 1 000 live births, South Africa - 25.8 deaths per 1 000 live births. There are reports that in 2021 nine birth centre clinics in Harare were shut down because of a shortage of midwives and with Zimbabwean nurses earning R 3 000 a month, many are leaving the country.

Press Release:


The scourge of xenophobia knows no boundaries. Pregnant women who aren't South African are being denied medical care because they cannot pay. They are called names and humiliated, but does the Health Act protect them?

Script:


VO: Motherhood, and the miracle of life. //
One of the most precious moments for a family. //
But what happens when the joy of bringing new life into this world is violated?

Betty: If someone goes to the hospital. You hear that such and such passed away, and you don't know what happened? Because they went to give birth, but didn't come back.

VO: This is Betty - // A Zimbabwean with a valid permit, working as a domestic worker in South Africa for over 20 years. In 2018 she went into labour with her third child and was rushed to Thembisa Hospital.
Betty: That was the toughest time. //

VO: It was during the ambulance drive that the paramedic gave Betty some alarming advice.

Betty: They say, listen because you're using a passport. I know these nurses are going to shout at you. So please don't say anything. Let them shout and keep quiet.

VO: At the hospital, she sat in a queue for many hours - finally she was ushered to a bed.

Betty: That's where I stayed for long hours,I can hear them passing. And I'm trying to scream to call please come and help me. And I was feeling like the baby's coming they were ignoring me

VO: Betty had had C-Sections before but her doctor gave her permission to try natural childbirth. The nurses seemed angry with her for making this choice.
Claire: Were you afraid?
Betty: I was very afraid. Because that's what they said, you will die on your bed, because you said you want to try normal birth. You will die on the bed.
BEAT// FOREBODING…

Nonkululeko: Obstetric violence is abuse, mistreatment or rights violations that occur when someone is either pregnant in the process of giving birth, or even postpartum.

VO: Nonkululeko Mbuli is the communications and advocacy strategist at Embrace, a social movement that champions mothers' rights.

Nonkululeko: The conversation around obstetric violence is growing momentum, particularly in relation to a concept that we call respectful maternity care. Obstetric violence is a kind of gender-based violence.

VO: Here, though, that violence often has a more sinister edge: xenophobia. Betty says she was singled out for being Zimbabwean.

Betty: They hear our language. Yeah, they say we are stubborn. if they talk to you and you reply them?. You ladies are coming from Zimbabwe are always like this.. They say names.

Nonkululeko: It plays out in many different ways.it could be the denial of care, it could be, you know, humiliating someone, discriminating them on the basis of their health status, as well as their nationality.

VO: The rights of foreign patients have recently made headlines, when a video of the MEC for health in Limpopo, Dr Phophi Ramathuba went viral.

Phopi Ramathuba video:
I'm operating with my limited budget.
You can't appreciate that.
You're killing my health system.

VO: She is berating an undocumented person for taking up subsidised health care she says, is meant for South Africans

Phopi Ramathuba video:
We are busy operating Mozambican nationals everywhere.
And you are not even registered. Anyway, you are not counted.
You're even illegal and you are abusing me.

VO: Her views were widely condemned in the medical community. // Dr Howard Manyonga an obstetrician and health care entrepreneur came to South Africa from Zimbabwe over 20 years ago. He says, as a doctor, Ramathuba, is bound by medical ethics.

Dr Manyonga: The Human Condition has got no nationality. This is a woman in need. And the duty of the doctor is to empathize, understand the human story. Let the system problems be dealt with at the political level.

VO: Dr Ramathuba's comments were inflammatory. Vigilante group, Operation Dudula, prevented foreign nationals from entering Gauteng's Kalafong Hospital.
(SOUND UP VIDEOS)
VO: and police had to intervene.
(sound up)
(beat//)
Sound up Ramathuba Twitterspace:
In Limpopo, we then have around 5.7 million people
VO: But Dr Ramathuba simply doubled down"
Sound up Ramathuba Twitterspace: Of those, 91% is dependent on the state. Now that tells you that whatever budget we have, already, it is overburdened.
VO: Using social media to defend herself.
Sound up Ramathuba Twitterspace:
Now the challenge becomes when you are not documented. This is where the overburdening of the system comes in. We are unable to bill them or to classify them. When the Auditor General audit us, we must prove why this person cannot pay.

VO: According to Dr Manyonga there is a misconception though, that all immigrants using public health care, are not paying for it.

Dr Manyonga: The total number of immigrants in this country is probably somewhere in the region of eight 10%. Provinces that closer to the border, will experience a disproportionate burden of the unbudgeted for clients.

Nonkululeko: It's important for us to explore the very systemic and very structural nature of the healthcare system that is currently in crisis. And, as opposed to looking for so-called scapegoats.

VO: Our questions about those systemic problems and whether foreign nationals are being scapegoated were ignored by the national Department of Health."

Nonkululeko: If you are a foreign woman, if you are undocumented, you are at higher risk of being mistreated and abused while seeking reproductive health care.

VO: And that was the case for 22-year-old undocumented migrant, Lizzie. At eight months pregnant her local clinic was unable to treat her further due to complications. She was told to go to Johannesburg's Charlotte Maxeke hospital.

Lizzie: When I go there for checkup. I showed him my paper. He asked me money. I tell him I don't have money. He say 5000, give me this paper.

VO: Lizzie was handed a document with the fee structure, but she couldn't even afford the R400 to take her blood pressure, never mind the R5000 for a checkup and R15 000 for delivery.

Claire: So what did they say when you said you didn't have money?
Lizzie: He say money sister, money.
Claire: Did they ask everyone to pay money?
Lizzie: Only foreigners.
(beat//)

LINK: There seems to be an inconsistency nationally around fees charged to foreign nationals seeking medical attention, or if any fees should be charged at all if they don't qualify through a means test.


VO: In other words, if they don't have money should they be charged? This is guided by the Uniform Patient Fee Schedule of hospital tariffs, while the means test determines which patients pay, what proportion, or if at all.

Nonkululeko: Accessing health care at a primary health care facility is free. So what usually happens is that the woman will be experiencing a high-risk pregnancy and will then be referred to a hospital, when she arrives at the hospital. She's then you know, confronted with these fees that she cannot afford to pay.

VO: The Gauteng Department of Health, in response to our questions about these fees, confirmed that our Constitution says that no one should be denied emergency care because they don't have money.
All public hospitals follow the same Gauteng DOH policy which is guided by the National Department of Health and in line with section 27 of the constitution that no patient may be denied emergency services because they do not have money.
VO: And it's the higher level of care hospitals where fees are being charged due to their specialist nature.
Services at Primary Health Care facilities (Clinics and Community Health Centres) are free of charge. It is the higher level of care at hospitals that is being charged mainly due to the specialist nature of the services.
VO: However, the National Health Act states, that if you are pregnant, or a child under the age of six you're entitled to free healthcare services, including at hospitals, for those not on medical aid and regardless of nationality
//Beat//
VO: The validity of this law is currently being tested in court.
Beat//

VO: The experience on the ground is evident.
Harry: She came outside, just past the stands here where they’re selling food, she collapses there

VO: Harry, a taxi marshal outside Rahima Moosa Mother and Child Hospital, west of Joburg, often helps pregnant women who've been denied care
Harry: I had to go back into the hospital to fetch a wheelchair. I take her back inside and I asked inside, why are you refusing this lady for treatment? Inside, they said, because she don't have money Because she's a foreigner.

VO: The Gauteng DOH urges the public to report these incidents.
We want to urge member of the public to report such incidents to us through the following channels:
Telephone: 0800 203 886 (Toll free number)
Email: patients.health@gauteng.gov.za/ support@gauteng.gov.za
SMS: 35023
Above this the Gauteng Provincial Service Delivery Hotline can also be used to lodge complaints: Via USSD *134*47472# or by calling 0800 228 827 or 0800 GAUTENG (4288364 with an extra digit).


Dr Manyonga: I guess the constitutional fathers understood that if you didn't provide primary health care services to everyone, it's a risk to everyone. Because you don't want to create reservoirs of unvaccinated children because sooner or later, that's an epidemic for everyone.

VO: So what are Lizzie's options when the system is hostile to her plight?

Claire: do you have a plan where you're going to have your baby?
Lizzie: I was thinking when I get money I'm going to I'm going to go back there
Claire: What if you don't get money?
Lizzie: I don't know huh... (silence)

Nonkululeko: this is a very clear rights violation, and we will be taking this up.

VO: Ultimately the protection of rights hinges on accountability, crucial to putting an end to society's cruelty towards the most vulnerable.

references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 16 October 2022 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 21 October 2022 Press Release: The scourge of xenophobia knows no boundaries. Pregnant women who aren't South African are being denied medical care because they cannot pay. They are called names and humiliated, but does the Health Act protect them? Script: VO: Motherhood, and the miracle of life. // One of the most precious moments for a family. // But what happens when the joy of bringing new life into this world is violated? Betty: If someone goes to the hospital. You hear that such and such passed away, and you don't know what happened? Because they went to give birth, but didn't come back. VO: This is Betty - // A Zimbabwean with a valid permit, working as a domestic worker in South Africa for over 20 years. In 2018 she went into labour with her third child and was rushed to Thembisa Hospital. Betty: That was the toughest time. // VO: It was during the ambulance drive that the paramedic gave Betty some alarming advice. Betty: They say, listen because you're using a passport. I know these nurses are going to shout at you. So please don't say anything. Let them shout and keep quiet. VO: At the hospital, she sat in a queue for many hours - finally she was ushered to a bed. Betty: That's where I stayed for long hours,I can hear them passing. And I'm trying to scream to call please come and help me. And I was feeling like the baby's coming they were ignoring me VO: Betty had had C-Sections before but her doctor gave her permission to try natural childbirth. The nurses seemed angry with her for making this choice. Claire: Were you afraid? Betty: I was very afraid. Because that's what they said, you will die on your bed, because you said you want to try normal birth. You will die on the bed. BEAT// FOREBODING… Nonkululeko: Obstetric violence is abuse, mistreatment or rights violations that occur when someone is either pregnant in the process of giving birth, or even postpartum. VO: Nonkululeko Mbuli is the communications and advocacy strategist at Embrace, a social movement that champions mothers' rights. Nonkululeko: The conversation around obstetric violence is growing momentum, particularly in relation to a concept that we call respectful maternity care. Obstetric violence is a kind of gender-based violence. VO: Here, though, that violence often has a more sinister edge: xenophobia. Betty says she was singled out for being Zimbabwean. Betty: They hear our language. Yeah, they say we are stubborn. if they talk to you and you reply them?. You ladies are coming from Zimbabwe are always like this.. They say names. Nonkululeko: It plays out in many different ways.it could be the denial of care, it could be, you know, humiliating someone, discriminating them on the basis of their health status, as well as their nationality. VO: The rights of foreign patients have recently made headlines, when a video of the MEC for health in Limpopo, Dr Phophi Ramathuba went viral. Phopi Ramathuba video: I'm operating with my limited budget. You can't appreciate that. You're killing my health system. VO: She is berating an undocumented person for taking up subsidised health care she says, is meant for South Africans Phopi Ramathuba video: We are busy operating Mozambican nationals everywhere. And you are not even registered. Anyway, you are not counted. You're even illegal and you are abusing me. VO: Her views were widely condemned in the medical community. // Dr Howard Manyonga an obstetrician and health care entrepreneur came to South Africa from Zimbabwe over 20 years ago. He says, as a doctor, Ramathuba, is bound by medical ethics. Dr Manyonga: The Human Condition has got no nationality. This is a woman in need. And the duty of the doctor is to empathize, understand the human story. Let the system problems be dealt with at the political level. VO: Dr Ramathuba's comments were inflammatory. Vigilante group, Operation Dudula, prevented foreign nationals from entering Gauteng's Kalafong Hospital. (SOUND UP VIDEOS) VO: and police had to intervene. (sound up) (beat//) Sound up Ramathuba Twitterspace: In Limpopo, we then have around 5.7 million people VO: But Dr Ramathuba simply doubled down" Sound up Ramathuba Twitterspace: Of those, 91% is dependent on the state. Now that tells you that whatever budget we have, already, it is overburdened. VO: Using social media to defend herself. Sound up Ramathuba Twitterspace: Now the challenge becomes when you are not documented. This is where the overburdening of the system comes in. We are unable to bill them or to classify them. When the Auditor General audit us, we must prove why this person cannot pay. VO: According to Dr Manyonga there is a misconception though, that all immigrants using public health care, are not paying for it. Dr Manyonga: The total number of immigrants in this country is probably somewhere in the region of eight 10%. Provinces that closer to the border, will experience a disproportionate burden of the unbudgeted for clients. Nonkululeko: It's important for us to explore the very systemic and very structural nature of the healthcare system that is currently in crisis. And, as opposed to looking for so-called scapegoats. VO: Our questions about those systemic problems and whether foreign nationals are being scapegoated were ignored by the national Department of Health." Nonkululeko: If you are a foreign woman, if you are undocumented, you are at higher risk of being mistreated and abused while seeking reproductive health care. VO: And that was the case for 22-year-old undocumented migrant, Lizzie. At eight months pregnant her local clinic was unable to treat her further due to complications. She was told to go to Johannesburg's Charlotte Maxeke hospital. Lizzie: When I go there for checkup. I showed him my paper. He asked me money. I tell him I don't have money. He say 5000, give me this paper. VO: Lizzie was handed a document with the fee structure, but she couldn't even afford the R400 to take her blood pressure, never mind the R5000 for a checkup and R15 000 for delivery. Claire: So what did they say when you said you didn't have money? Lizzie: He say money sister, money. Claire: Did they ask everyone to pay money? Lizzie: Only foreigners. (beat//) LINK: There seems to be an inconsistency nationally around fees charged to foreign nationals seeking medical attention, or if any fees should be charged at all if they don't qualify through a means test. VO: In other words, if they don't have money should they be charged? This is guided by the Uniform Patient Fee Schedule of hospital tariffs, while the means test determines which patients pay, what proportion, or if at all. Nonkululeko: Accessing health care at a primary health care facility is free. So what usually happens is that the woman will be experiencing a high-risk pregnancy and will then be referred to a hospital, when she arrives at the hospital. She's then you know, confronted with these fees that she cannot afford to pay. VO: The Gauteng Department of Health, in response to our questions about these fees, confirmed that our Constitution says that no one should be denied emergency care because they don't have money. All public hospitals follow the same Gauteng DOH policy which is guided by the National Department of Health and in line with section 27 of the constitution that no patient may be denied emergency services because they do not have money. VO: And it's the higher level of care hospitals where fees are being charged due to their specialist nature. Services at Primary Health Care facilities (Clinics and Community Health Centres) are free of charge. It is the higher level of care at hospitals that is being charged mainly due to the specialist nature of the services. VO: However, the National Health Act states, that if you are pregnant, or a child under the age of six you're entitled to free healthcare services, including at hospitals, for those not on medical aid and regardless of nationality //Beat// VO: The validity of this law is currently being tested in court. Beat// VO: The experience on the ground is evident. Harry: She came outside, just past the stands here where they’re selling food, she collapses there VO: Harry, a taxi marshal outside Rahima Moosa Mother and Child Hospital, west of Joburg, often helps pregnant women who've been denied care Harry: I had to go back into the hospital to fetch a wheelchair. I take her back inside and I asked inside, why are you refusing this lady for treatment? Inside, they said, because she don't have money Because she's a foreigner. VO: The Gauteng DOH urges the public to report these incidents. We want to urge member of the public to report such incidents to us through the following channels: Telephone: 0800 203 886 (Toll free number) Email: patients.health@gauteng.gov.za/ support@gauteng.gov.za SMS: 35023 Above this the Gauteng Provincial Service Delivery Hotline can also be used to lodge complaints: Via USSD *134*47472# or by calling 0800 228 827 or 0800 GAUTENG (4288364 with an extra digit). Dr Manyonga: I guess the constitutional fathers understood that if you didn't provide primary health care services to everyone, it's a risk to everyone. Because you don't want to create reservoirs of unvaccinated children because sooner or later, that's an epidemic for everyone. VO: So what are Lizzie's options when the system is hostile to her plight? Claire: do you have a plan where you're going to have your baby? Lizzie: I was thinking when I get money I'm going to I'm going to go back there Claire: What if you don't get money? Lizzie: I don't know huh... (silence) Nonkululeko: this is a very clear rights violation, and we will be taking this up. VO: Ultimately the protection of rights hinges on accountability, crucial to putting an end to society's cruelty towards the most vulnerable.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Hospitals have become the latest epicentre of xenophobic friction. Is the unconstitutional maltreatment of foreign pregnant women in South African medical facilities fuellin the fire of xenophobia?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: And what of the victims? All over various media we’ve seen Dr Phophi Ramathuba MEC for Health in Limpopo, lambasting a Zimbabwean patient for taking up bed space and resources in a Limpopo Hospital. She further rants, that the Zimbabwian government should be paying for her. She makes an example of her recent trip to Canada, and goes on to say, that if she were to fall ill there, she would have to pay for it. Her entourage laughs with her as she continues to berate the patient. Before you know it, Operation Dudula are trying to prevent foreigners from entering Kalafong Hospital in Attridgeville, asking for their permits and papers and refusing them entrance if they are foreign. A stand-off and violence erupt as EFF oppose this action. But medical xenophobia has been an ongoing problem in South Africa and over the last couple of years it has been even more evident in labour wards. Here women are mistreated because they are foreigners but are too afraid to speak out. Not only do they fear for their own life but the unborn baby they are bringing into the world. Section 4(3) of the National Health Act says "All pregnant and breastfeeding women and children under the age of six are eligible for free health care services at public clinics or hospitals." In this very personal story of pain and humiliation we explore the indignity that befalls women of foreign origin at the hands of South Africa’s public health care system in the wake of xenophobic rhetoric which is escalating conveniently and alarmingly before elections.
metadata.Summary: Gertie, a Zimbabwian woman who wishes to remain anonymous. Has been living and working in South Africa as a domestic for the last 20 years. She fell pregnant with her 3rd child in South Africa three years ago. She went to Thembisa Hospital for obstetric care. Even as she got into the ambulance while in labour, the Venda ambulance driver warned her that they don’t like foreigners at the hospital, and that if she was goaded or badly treated she should keep quiet and not incite the hospital staff, as it would be even more dangerous for her. Gertie wanted to have natural child birth, but it was at this point that the nursing staff started to threaten her, saying if she were to have natural childbirth, they would leave her to die, referring to her as “these Zimbabwian women are very stubborn”. Gertie felt humiliated and afraid, not knowing if she was going to live or die, giving birth to her daughter. She did what the paramedic told her to do, and when she was shouted at, she just kept quiet. She gave birth to a beautiful daughter, but never went back to the hospital for any post natal care. Subsequently because of all the xenophobia, she sent her other children back to Zimbabwe, fearing for their lives. This is one story of many women who are suffering in South Africa’s obstetric health care. Many are crying out that this is unconstitutional and inhumane. Activists are angry and point to the constitution that all people should have access to healthcare even if they are undocumented or foreign. Prof Alex Van den Heever condemns these actions, and blames it on a lack of policy that was never put in place in 1994 in conjunction with neigbouring counties.
metadata.Further information: The knock-on effect according to Dr Manyonga, a Zimbabwean obstetrician resident in South Africa for over 20 years, is that women are opting for back-room or home births, which in itself causes complications. Moreover after giving birth these foreign nationals don’t get their children immunised for fear of being victimised. In the long term this could cause serious health hazards for the entire population. Like an outbreak of measles. We explore the route of this deep seated xenophobia and why pregnant mothers are particularly vulnerable, we challenge the Department of Health on their perspective and why Dr Ramathuba’s comments although they may be vested in truth, go against the Hippocratic Oath and is this a culture in health care that the department is willing to perpetuate? Dr Manyonga wants to be part of a solution, realising a few years back how inefficient obstetric treatment is in the public sector, not only for foreign women but mainly for South African women, he set up an entire service, which extends to engagements with private clinics and the services of midwives, creating a network of affordable obstetric care. His venture was curtailed during COVID, but now it is back in full swing, and what he has found is that more and more foreign women are seeking this service for fear of what lies in the public sector hospitals. Dr Manyonga is concerned with Dr Ramathuba’s comments, particularly as he states, that was a conversation that should have been had at a higher level, rather than breaking the patient doctor confidentiality. He also addresses the deeper reasons for this influx of patients from Zimbabwe, as the health care system there is virtually nonexistent. Doula Bev, knows first hand of incidents of maltreatment. She wants to remain anonymous, but can attest to the many instances of maltreatment of women she has helped ( I may not interview her, if I can get an on camera interview with a midwife that I am trying to get hold of) I am hoping Flora Banda will give us an interview even though it will probably also be anonymous, concerning a member of her family who they say died shortly after giving birth to twins due to hospital neglect. She was a Malawian national and undocumented. Yolanda Dumpson, whose story was covered by Health-E, is worried about speaking more because she now fears xenophobic attacks – but it looks like we have other case studies of our own. Sibongile Tshabalala from Treatment Action Campaign (TAC) who are condemning this inhumane treatment of people. Sibongile can be interviewed as an activist. As an expert, Professor Alex Van Den Heever, says the problem is that since 1994 there no policy has been defined between the SADC countries and this needs to be addressed by government. The National Department of Health needs to address the issues of what happened this week. Why was the MEC allowed to speak the way she did? Why is there is so much xenophobia, and what is their position, especially, what is being done to protect pregnant women who constitutionally should be able to expect equal healthcare in South African public hospitals We can narrow down the interviews in frying session so that there are not too many. As Carte Blanche highlighted during its medical series, South Africa’s national health system is suffering from dysfunctionality... a baby is about to be born and in many cases hospital staff are more worried about nationality, ids, hospital cards and paperwork than they are about the welfare of mother and baby. It’s not like a woman about to give birth is arriving at a hospital with a cough. Is it endemic corruption because it siphons off much needed funding? Or are foreigners using up resources meant for South Africans? Many citizens blame foreign patients for the lack of care afforded them. And the tensions are starting to boil. Opponents to this attitude are groups that quote our constitution - Section 27 of South Africa's Constitution states the right to access health care services is one of the basic human rights for everyone. This includes reproductive health care services. Others campaign for tighter border controls to ease the issue of illegal foreigners. Whatever the argument or motivation, the fallout is being felt most harshly by the vulnerable. And if you were in their position would you have stayed in Zimbabwe for instance or seek care elsewhere? The Zimbabwean health system has crumbled and hard hit are expectant mothers... United Nations data shows that there are 37.9 deaths per 1 000 live births in Zimbabwe. A stark contrast to data for Zimbabwe's neighbours... in Botswana - 28.8 deaths per 1 000 live births, South Africa - 25.8 deaths per 1 000 live births. There are reports that in 2021 nine birth centre clinics in Harare were shut down because of a shortage of midwives and with Zimbabwean nurses earning R 3 000 a month, many are leaving the country.
